title: Numeral Systems Across Languages Support Efficient Communication: From Approximate Numerosity to Recursion

claims.statement: Attested numeral systems (30 languages: approximate, exact restricted, recursive) tend to be more informative than most hypothetical systems of the same complexity, i.e. they are near-optimally efficient; the result depends on a need distribution that decreases with magnitude and fails under uniform need.
claims.scope: Numbers 1-100; need = English Google-ngram numeral frequencies smoothed to 0.6182 x^-2.02; complexity = symbols in a hand-written grammar; listener models grounded in subitizing / Weber's law / exact numerosity; evidence is visual (Fig. 3A), no test statistic.

quantities.name: placements_of_3_exact_terms_beating_the_prefix
quantities.unit: placements of 3 exact singleton terms on 1..100 (residual = one 'higher' term) with lower expected cost than {1,2,3}
quantities.baseline: same for k = 2 (0/4,950) and, in 20,000 random placements, k = 4 and 6; holds for a Bayesian and a uniform residual listener

quantities.name: need_mass_on_numbers_1_to_3
quantities.unit: share of total communicative need (paper's power law) on 1..3

quantities.name: attested_exact_restricted_on_hypothetical_frontier_by_construction
quantities.unit: coded exact-restricted languages whose (complexity, cost) equals the hypothetical prefix frontier point at the same k
quantities.baseline: the frontier and the attested cost are the same function of k; the paper lists 18 exact-restricted languages, the deposit codes 17 (no Krenak)

quantities.name: attested_exact_restricted_dominated_by_prefix_systems
quantities.unit: coded exact-restricted languages with a prefix system of lower-or-equal complexity and lower cost
quantities.baseline: Hup dominated by 2 (k = 21, 22), Waskia by 7 (k = 11..17); the two with composed numerals

our_assessment.why: Sharpened 2026-11-12 with the deposit (reanalysis/n2): for exact-restricted systems the paper's 'near-optimal' is an identity. The code scores an attested exact-restricted language as compute_cost_size_principle(ulim), a function of its upper limit alone, and draws the hypothetical 'efficient' exact curve with the SAME function at every k; complexity of a hypothetical prefix system is a formula (3k+4 up to k=3, then 13+4(k-3)). 15 of the 17 coded exact-restricted languages have exactly that complexity, so each attested point IS a frontier point. Every k is Pareto-optimal among prefix systems, so the model cannot say why a language stops at 3 rather than 5 or 10. The only two exact-restricted languages whose grammar departs from the formula -- Hup (ulim 20, complexity 89 vs 81) and Waskia (ulim 10, 69 vs 41), both with composed numerals -- are DOMINATED by 2 and 7 prefix systems respectively in the paper's own measure. So in the null that matters (systems that count from one), the class carries no evidence for efficiency, and the only non-trivial cases point mildly against it. 2026-10-16 analytic result kept: under the paper's need (84% on 1-3) the prefix placement of k exact terms is the optimum among all placements (0/161,700 for k=3). Recursive systems (cost 0 by construction) and approximate systems are not touched by this check.

checked.result: Code and data for the whole analysis (Python 2-era, Cython routines, need files, per-language grammars). The main block as deposited draws the uniform-need supplementary figure (configuration, not a defect). langstrategy.py codes 25 of the paper's 30 languages: Krenak (exact), Chiquitano and Fuyuge (approximate), French and Spanish (recursive) are absent. Hypothetical systems are not stored; they are regenerated (only the cheapest and dearest of each class are generated for restricted systems).

relations.why: Same programme and the same missing null: the class-defining structure (here, exact terms as a prefix of the number line) already delivers the efficiency under the assumed need.
Need distribution estimated from usage of the very terms whose efficiency is being judged (English numerals; WCS naming data for the LI prior).

open_questions: ANSWERED 2026-11-12 (reanalysis/n2, OSF deposit a1): restricted to prefix-respecting hypothetical systems, the exact-restricted comparison has zero discriminating power. 15/17 attested systems coincide with the frontier by construction, and the 2 with composed numerals (Hup, Waskia) are dominated. See c1.

Does efficiency discriminate WHICH k languages choose (3 vs 4 vs 6) beyond the prefix shape? With cost falling monotonically in k and complexity rising, any k is on the frontier -- variation across languages is not explained by the model.

The deposit codes 25 of the 30 languages in Table 1 (absent: Krenak, Chiquitano, Fuyuge, French, Spanish), yet Figures 3-5 plot all 30. Were the other five scored by code that is not in the deposit? Figure points cannot be regenerated for them from a1.

Figure 3's caption says Rama, Barasano, Imonda and Yidiny have 'terms for the first six numerals and a higher term'; the deposit gives all four ulim = 5 (exact 1..5, 'higher' from 6). Caption wording, or a different coding from the one plotted?

CHECKED AND WITHDRAWN 2026-11-12 (do not re-find): in 11 of the 17 exact-restricted grammars the HIG rule reuses the top exact numeral's form (e.g. Achagua 'matalii' for 3 and 4..100), while the cost assumes ulim is exact. reanalysis/n4: calc_complexity is 13 with the reused form and 13 with a distinct invented form, so inside the model the string is a placeholder, and both cost and complexity describe 'k exact terms + a distinct higher term', as the caption says. Not a defect. Whether these languages' top numeral also means 'more' is a linguistic question the model cannot represent; not checked against the grammars cited.
